description_full: IDEX Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, provides applied solutions in the United States, North America, Europe, Asia, and internationally. It operates through three segments: Health & Science Technologies (HST), Fluid & Metering Technologies (FMT) and Fire & Safety/Diversified Products (FSDP). The HST segment designs, produces, and distributes a range of precision fluidics, positive displacement pumps, powder and liquid processing technologies, drying systems, micro-precision components, pneumatic components and sealing solutions, high performance molded and extruded sealing components, and custom mechanical and shaft seals. This segment also offers engineered hygienic mixers and valves, biocompatible medical devices and implantable products, air compressors and blowers, optical components and coatings, ultra-precision diamond tools, and laboratory and commercial equipment, as well as precision photonic solutions, technical ceramics, hermetic sealing products, porous material structures, and flow control solutions. The FMT segment designs, produces, and distributes positive displacement pumps, valves, small volume provers, flow meters, injectors, other fluid-handling pump modules, and systems; and provides flow monitoring and other services. The FSDP segment designs, produces, and distributes firefighting pumps, valves and controls, and rescue tools; lifting bags and other components and systems; engineered stainless steel banding and clamping devices; and precision equipment for dispensing, metering, and mixing colorants and paints. The company was incorporated in 1987 and is headquartered in Northbrook, Illinois.

financial_summary: IDEX Corporation is a large-cap industrials business with a $17.5B market cap on $3.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 14% against a 8% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 44%.

The business throws off $617M in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.41× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.6× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 9.7×.

Shareholder yield of 2.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Trading near 52-week highs — the market has already recognised the story (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)
Significant goodwill (49% of assets) from past acquisitions — a soft asset a conservative appraisal discounts to zero
Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 6% over 3 months
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

Piotroski score 7/9 — financials improving across profitability, leverage and efficiency
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
31 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible

sect: Its 20% operating margin runs 11pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.82x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-5.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 44% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 23% and a beta of 0.85, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $151.9M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 36% in the 2020 crash, 26% in the 2022 bear market and 58% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $195 (margin of safety -22%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 36%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $150 to $256 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 33.0 vs 24.1 and EV/EBITDA 18.7 vs 13.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 23% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 14 covering analysts target $263 on average, 11% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 14% earns above the cost of capital of 8.5%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.29).
It runs a 44% gross margin and converts 18% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.41x.
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.0% of revenue on R&D and 0.8% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.6x net debt to EBITDA ($580.0M of cash against $1.8B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 9.7x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.5, in the safe zone).
Goodwill makes up 49% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.8% over 3 years, 8.0% over 5 years and 5.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 17% of profits supports about 2.4% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 3.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.8x, 1.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 25, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 2.6% a year to shareholders (1.4% in buybacks and 1.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 31 consecutive years, raising it 7.0% a year over the last five.
people: With about 8,700 employees, each generates about $397K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 5.7% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $71K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.7M (7x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
